claims.text: Applying a silicide-based surface coating to boride-based components will substantially improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion.
The silicide coating will improve corrosion resistance by forming a protective diffusion barrier.
The relevant uncoated boride components have a dense native boride microstructure.
Pack cementation or a similar process can be used to deposit a silicide coating.
The deposited coating will be thin and uniform on the boride component.
Typical hot-dip aluminum-plating exposure temperatures are approximately 700–800°C.
The coating must remain adherent and intact during thermal cycling and thermal-expansion mismatch to remain protective.
The coating will have a dense two-layer structure consisting of a primary MSi2 layer and an underlying MSi layer.
The two-layer silicide coating will limit aluminum diffusion into the boride substrate.
Stable aluminide phases may form and self-heal minor defects in the coating.
The silicide layer will slow penetration of molten aluminum into the underlying boride.
In-situ formation of aluminide or oxide particles may fill minor cracks in the coating.
Self-healing has been observed in silicide-coated systems under oxidation conditions.
Silicide-coated components will have significantly lower weight loss than uncoated boride components during comparable molten-aluminum exposure.
Silicide-coated components will have shallower corrosion penetration than uncoated boride components during comparable molten-aluminum exposure.
Uncoated boride components undergo higher corrosion rates because they interact directly with molten aluminum.
Nonuniform coating, insufficient thickness, poor adhesion, excessive thermal-expansion mismatch, or coating degradation could diminish or eliminate the protective benefit.
